question: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician with a 1-week history of sharp, substernal chest pain that is worse with inspiration and relieved with leaning forward. He has also had nausea and myalgias. His father has coronary artery disease. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 130/84 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a high-pitched rubbing sound between S1 and S2 that is best heard at the left sternal border. An ECG shows depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Sharp, substernal chest pain worse with inspiration and relieved with leaning forward" -> "Pericarditis likely" -> "High-pitched rubbing sound on cardiac exam" -> "Pericardial friction rub present" -> "ECG shows depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations" -> "Pericarditis with ECG changes" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Father has coronary artery disease" -> "Increased risk for cardiovascular conditions" -> "Consideration of pericarditis in differential diagnosis" -> "Symptoms and ECG findings consistent with pericarditis" -> 90%
enhanced_information: The patient's symptoms of sharp, substernal chest pain worse with inspiration and relieved with leaning forward, along with a high-pitched rubbing sound on cardiac exam and ECG changes of depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations, are highly suggestive of pericarditis. Given the family history of coronary artery disease, pericarditis should be considered in the differential diagnosis. Dressler syndrome is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms.
analysis: The patient's presentation with sharp substernal chest pain worsened by inspiration, relieved by leaning forward, along with a pericardial friction rub, and ECG changes of depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations are classic findings of acute pericarditis. Dressler syndrome is a delayed post-myocardial infarction syndrome and would not present acutely with these symptoms. Acute myocardial infarction typically presents with different ECG changes and is less likely given the clinical picture. Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and systemic lupus erythematosus are less likely based on the presentation. Acute viral infection is a broad category and does not fit the specific findings in this case.
